\chapter{Una carta del colegio}
\label{ch:es-informe}
\hlchaptermodality{466}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read a formal letter home from a school: understand who signed it, what it reports about behaviour, that the change can be seen, and that being asked to discuss something is an invitation rather than a summons.}

Read a letter home from the head, then say what it actually asks for.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el director / la directora]{el director — the one who signs the letter}

\label{lesson:ES-C466-director}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{directo} and \textbf{el actor}. One gave you the verb and one gave you the ending. Put them together and you have this word already.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el director}
\textbf{el director}, \textbf{la directora} — the head, the director.

\begin{quote}
Atentamente, la \textbf{directora} del centro.
\end{quote}

\emph{El director del colegio} — the head teacher. \emph{La directora de la empresa} — the company director. \emph{El director de cine} — the film director.

Unlike \emph{el guía}, this one \textbf{does} change: \emph{director}, \emph{directora}. It ends in a consonant, so the feminine adds \textbf{-a} rather than moving the article.

\begin{cousinweb}
You have been given both halves already, in two different chapters, and this is where they meet.

When you learned \textbf{el actor}, the \emph{-tor} ending was set out as Latin's way of naming the doer: take a verb, add \emph{-tor}, get the one who does it. The table there listed \emph{agere $\to$ actor}, \emph{docere $\to$ doctor} — and \textbf{dirigere $\to$ director}. The word was printed in front of you before you needed it.

Then \textbf{directo} gave you \emph{dirigere} itself: to set something straight, to aim it. So a \emph{director} is the one who \textbf{aims the thing} — not the one who shouts, the one who points it where it is going.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the verb} & \textbf{the doer} \\
\midrule
dirigere, to aim & el director \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Dirigir} is the living Spanish verb: \emph{dirigir una empresa}, to run a company. And \emph{dirigirse a alguien} is to address somebody — to aim your words at a person, which is what the letter in this chapter does.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the head teacher, then the headmistress
  \item what dirigere means
  \item the ending that names the doer
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The head? (\textbf{El director} — \emph{la directora}.) What does a director do to a thing? (\textbf{Aims it} — \emph{dirigere}, to set straight.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[visible]{visible — able to be seen}

\label{lesson:ES-C466-visible}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{sociable} and \textbf{el aviso}. One gave you the ending, the other gave you the root. This word is the two of them stuck together.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: visible}
\textbf{visible} — visible, able to be seen.

\begin{quote}
El aviso debe quedar \textbf{visible} en el tablón.
\end{quote}

\emph{En un lugar visible} — somewhere it can be seen, the phrase notices use about themselves. \emph{Una mejora visible} — a noticeable improvement.

Like \emph{sociable}, it has \textbf{one form for everyone}: \emph{un cartel visible}, \emph{una puerta visible}. Adjectives in this family do not take a feminine.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: -able and -ible point two ways}]
They are one ending, Latin \textbf{-bilis}, wearing two spellings. Which vowel you get depends on the Latin verb it was built from, and there is no rule worth memorising — you learn each word.

What is worth noticing is the \textbf{direction}, because it is not fixed either:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{adjective} & \textbf{who is doing what} \\
\midrule
sociable & the person \textbf{does} the mixing \\
visible & somebody else \textbf{does} the seeing \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Sociable} describes a person inclined to do something. \emph{Visible} describes a thing that can have something done to it. The ending covers both, and only the sense of the verb tells you which way it points — \emph{un niño sociable} mixes, \emph{un cartel visible} is looked at.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{videre}, to see — the root you met under \emph{el aviso}, where \emph{a-vis-o} turned out to be \emph{ad visum}, \textquotedblleft{}to what is seen\textquotedblright{}.

The same \emph{videre} is under a great many English words, and they arrived by different doors: \textbf{vision} and \textbf{visible} and \textbf{evident} came through Latin, while \textbf{advice} came through French and \textbf{view} came through French from the same place. Spanish keeps \emph{ver} as the everyday verb and saves \emph{videre}'s own shape for the formal words: \emph{visible}, \emph{la visión}, \emph{evidente}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item it must stay visible on the board
  \item which of sociable and visible has it done to them
  \item the Latin verb underneath
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Visible? (\textbf{Visible} — one form for everyone.) Does it change for a feminine noun? (\textbf{No}.) The Latin verb? (\emph{\textbf{Videre}}, to see.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el comportamiento]{el comportamiento — how somebody carries themselves}

\label{lesson:ES-C466-comportamiento}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{importar} and \textbf{el aparcamiento}. One holds the root of the next word and the other holds its ending.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el comportamiento}
\textbf{el comportamiento} — behaviour, conduct.

\begin{quote}
Su \textbf{comportamiento} en clase ha mejorado.
\end{quote}

\emph{El comportamiento del grupo} — the group's behaviour. In a school letter it is the formal word; a parent at home is more likely to say \emph{se porta bien} or \emph{se porta mal}.

\textbf{Comportarse} is the verb: \emph{compórtate}, behave yourself.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{com-}, together, plus \textbf{portare}, to carry — the \emph{portare} you had under \emph{importar}, where carrying something \textbf{in} turned out to be the whole of what Rome meant by it.

To \emph{comportarse} is to \textbf{carry yourself}, and English does the identical thing: \emph{conduct} is \emph{con-} plus \emph{ducere}, to lead — to lead yourself. Two languages, two verbs of motion, the same idea that character is something you are carrying about.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
comportarse, to carry oneself & to conduct oneself \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Keep it away from \emph{la puerta}. That is \emph{porta}, a gate, and the warning came with \emph{importar}: the two look alike and are not the same word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: -miento on a reflexive verb}]
You have \textbf{-miento} from \emph{el aparcamiento}: an ending that makes a noun out of a verb. This one is built on \emph{comportarse}, which is reflexive, and the noun quietly drops the \emph{se}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{noun} \\
\midrule
aparcar & el aparcamiento \\
comportarse & el comportamiento \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So the noun names the carrying without saying whose. That is exactly what a school letter wants: \emph{el comportamiento} is a fact about conduct, where \emph{se porta mal} is an accusation about a child.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item his behaviour in class has improved
  \item behave yourself
  \item what com- plus portare means literally
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Behaviour? (\textbf{El comportamiento}.) The verb? (\textbf{Comportarse}.) What are you carrying? (\textbf{Yourself}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[discutir]{discutir — to discuss, and to argue}

\label{lesson:ES-C466-discutir}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la reunión} and \textbf{el director}. A meeting with the head is where this verb usually turns up.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: discutir}
\textbf{discutir} — to discuss, and also to argue.

\begin{quote}
Podemos \textbf{discutir} el comportamiento en la reunión.
\end{quote}

\emph{Discutir un tema} — to discuss a topic. \emph{Discutir con alguien} — to argue with somebody. \textbf{La discusión} is both the discussion and the row.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the preposition decides}]
One verb covers what English splits between \emph{discuss} and \emph{argue}, and the grammar around it does most of the sorting.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what follows} & \textbf{what it means} \\
\midrule
a thing — \emph{discutir el precio} & discuss it \\
\textbf{con} a person — \emph{discutir con él} & argue with him \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A thing after the verb is a topic; a person after \textbf{con} is an opponent. It is not watertight — \emph{discutir el precio con el jefe} can be either, and tone settles it — but the pattern is reliable enough to lean on, and mistaking the two is how a polite sentence turns rude.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{discutere}: \textbf{dis-}, apart, plus \textbf{quatere}, to shake.

To \emph{discutere} was to \textbf{shake a thing to pieces} — to strike it until it came apart and you could see what was inside. The Romans used it of smashing, and only later of taking an argument apart.

Which makes the two Spanish senses one sense. Discussing a topic and arguing with a person are the same act at two temperatures: something is being shaken until it comes apart. English kept the violent end elsewhere — \textbf{concussion} is \emph{con-} plus the same \emph{quatere}, a shaking-together of the head.

\emph{Percusión} is the third member, the shaking-through of a struck drum.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item we can discuss the behaviour at the meeting
  \item to argue with somebody
  \item what quatere means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To discuss? (\textbf{Discutir}.) And with a person, using \emph{con}? (\textbf{To argue}.) What did \emph{quatere} do? (\textbf{Shook} — \emph{discutere} shakes a thing apart.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(el director, visible, el …]{(el director, visible, el comportamiento, discutir) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R466-repaso-informe}



\begin{quote}
Four words, no prompts. Who signs the letter, what the notice must stay, what the letter is about, and what the meeting will do with it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the four, cold}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{English} & \textbf{Spanish} \\
\midrule
the head & \textbf{el director} \\
visible & \textbf{visible} \\
behaviour & \textbf{el comportamiento} \\
to discuss, to argue & \textbf{discutir} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three endings you already had}]
Not one of this chapter's endings is new. What is new is which way each one bends.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ending} & \textbf{does it change for a woman?} \\
\midrule
\textbf{-tor} & yes — \emph{director}, \emph{directora} \\
\textbf{-ible} & no — \emph{visible} for everyone \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{El actor} gave you \emph{-tor} and printed \emph{director} in its own table. \emph{Sociable} gave you the \emph{-able} half of \emph{-ible} and the rule that it has one form. \emph{El aparcamiento} gave you \emph{-miento}. The chapter is four words and nothing underneath them you had not already been handed.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Two of the four are about \textbf{carrying and shaking}, which is not what a school letter sounds like.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{what is underneath} \\
\midrule
el comportamiento & \emph{com-} + \emph{portare} — carrying yourself \\
discutir & \emph{dis-} + \emph{quatere} — shaking a thing apart \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{El director} aims (\emph{dirigere}, to set straight) and \emph{visible} is seen (\emph{videre}). Four abstractions, four physical verbs, and the letter that uses all four is about a child in a classroom.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the headmistress wants to discuss his behaviour
  \item it must stay visible
  \item which two of the four change for a woman
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The head? (\textbf{El director}.) Visible? (\textbf{Visible}.) Behaviour? (\textbf{El comportamiento}.) To discuss? (\textbf{Discutir}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(una carta del colegio) — read it, then say what it wants}

\label{lesson:ES-C466-sintesis-informe}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el director} and \textbf{el comportamiento}. A letter with both words in it is rarely good news, and rarely as bad as it looks.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=orange!6,colframe=orange!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Read this}]
\begin{quote}
Estimada familia:
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Les escribo para informarles de que el \textbf{comportamiento} de su hijo en clase ha mejorado de forma \textbf{visible} durante este trimestre.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Me gustaría \textbf{discutir} con ustedes cómo mantener esa mejora. Pueden pedir cita en secretaría.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Atentamente,
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
La \textbf{directora}
\end{quote}
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what the letter is not doing}]
A reader who knows \emph{discutir} only as \emph{argue} will read this as a summons. It is not one, and two words tell you so.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the word} & \textbf{what it settles} \\
\midrule
\emph{ha mejorado} & the news is good \\
\emph{discutir} \textbf{con ustedes} & a conversation, not a row \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Discutir con} was given as the arguing shape, and here it is doing the other job — because what is being discussed is an improvement. That is the limit of the rule: the preposition leans, the content decides.

Note also \textbf{de forma visible}. The letter does not say the child is visible; it says the improvement can be seen. \emph{Visible} is passive, as its ending warned.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say in one sentence what the letter reports and what it asks for.

Now say the same news to a friend, out of the formal register: start with \emph{se porta} instead of \emph{el comportamiento}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Who wrote it? (\textbf{La directora}.) What improved? (\textbf{El comportamiento}.) How much? (\textbf{De forma visible}.) What does she want? (\textbf{Discutir} — to talk it over.)
\end{tcolorbox}
